title: An Autonomous Generate→Verify→Repair (GVR) Pipeline for Intent-to-Configuration Safety in NetOps: A Confirmatory, Paired Evaluation with gpt-5-mini
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, autonomous, paired experiment that evaluated whether an end-to-end generate→verify→repair (GVR) pipeline reduces emulator-confirmed safety violations in LLM-produced network configurations. Using preregistration study-gvr-2026-001, we sampled 100 public natural-language NetOps intents stratified by vendor family and ran a within-intent paired comparison (LLM-only baseline vs. GVR-guarded) with gpt-5-mini, a deterministic rule-based verifier (reachability / ACL / forwarding-loop / explicit-policy checks), and Mininet-based emulation. Ninety-nine intent pairs completed. Baseline produced 97/99 non-violating intents; the GVR pipeline produced 99/99 non-violating intents (paired absolute improvement = 0.0202). Exact McNemar (two-sided) on the discordant pairs (n_10=2, n_01=0) yields p=0.5; paired bootstrap-percentile 95% CI for the difference (10k resamples, seed=1729) is [0.000, 0.0505]. The preregistered target (≥30 percentage-point absolute reduction) was not achieved. We release the full preregistration, prompts, raw LLM responses, verifier reports, emulator logs, and analysis code (artifact hashes in the execution manifest) to enable audit and reproduction. We interpret the near-null confirmatory result, analyze failure modes, and discuss practical implications and next steps for operational GVR adoption.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are being proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent-to-configuration translation. Their stochastic generation, however, can produce misconfigurations or unsafe changes with operational impact. Generate→Verify→Repair (GVR) architectures interpose deterministic oracles to bound stochastic outputs and permit automated repair loops; prior work proposes such pipelines for regulatory and production settings (see Convergent Correctness / GVR literature). We conducted a preregistered confirmatory experiment to answer: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM + deterministic network verifier + emulator confirmation) materially reduce emulator-confirmed safety violations compared to LLM-only generation? Our contributions: (1) an archived preregistered paired trial (study-gvr-2026-001) with public artifacts; (2) a deterministic analysis showing realized effect and uncertainty; (3) a failure-mode and operational implications analysis that identifies where GVR has practical leverage.
sections.related_work: We situate this study at the intersection of LLM-driven NetOps, retrieval/tool-augmented correctness workflows, and deterministic network verification. Work on intent-based translation with LLMs demonstrates feasibility but often lacks deterministic operational checks. RAG and verifier-augmented systems (surveys on RAG and verifier pipelines) show grounding reduces hallucination; work on Generate-Verify-Repair for code and regulated domains shows the architecture can convert stochastic proposals into verifiable outputs. Network-verification tools (e.g., VeriFlow and related rule-based checkers) demonstrate online invariant checking feasibility in SDN contexts. Our experiment operationalizes a bounded GVR loop under a strict preregistered budget and emulator confirmation to provide empirical evidence on GVR effectiveness for public NetOps intents.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. The full preregistration (study-gvr-2026-001) was frozen before any model calls and is archived in the execution bundle. Design: paired within-intent comparison (baseline LLM-only vs. guarded GVR) on 100 public English NetOps intents stratified by vendor (Cisco=34, Juniper=33, Arista=33). Inclusion/exclusion, contamination detection, stopping rules, and retry policy followed the preregistered plan. Pipeline. LLM: gpt-5-mini (hosted). Generation used a shared initial candidate prompt per intent; the guarded condition ran the same initial generation plus deterministic verification of the candidate and, when the verifier flagged a violation, performed a single preregistered repair call that injected typed verifier diagnostics into a repair prompt (maximum 1 repair call per intent as pre-specified). Verifier. Deterministic rule set covering: reachability violations, ACL semantics and ordering contradictions, forwarding-loop detection, and explicit policy contradictions. Emulation. Mininet-based topologies in Docker containers were used to confirm whether a verifier-flagged issue manifested as an emulator-observed operational failure. Scoring. An intent is scored as 'success' if the final configuration produced no verifier-flagged, emulator-confirmed safety violation. Primary estimand: paired absolute difference in success proportions (guarded minus baseline). Statistical analysis (pre-specified). Primary test: exact McNemar two-sided on discordant pair counts (n_10, n_01) with the exact conditional/binomial formulation; no mid-p correction was applied. Confidence intervals: paired bootstrap-percentile for the difference (10,000 resamples, seed=1729), resampling pairs (complete-pair resampling) and respecting preregistered missingness/exclusion rules. Reproducibility. All prompts, raw LLM responses, verifier outputs, emulator logs, and analysis code (deterministic Dockerized analysis) are archived; critical artifact hashes (paired contingency table, contamination summary, bootstrap seed) are included in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution accounting. The run executed autonomously per the preregistration. Planned episodes = 200 (100 intents × 2 conditions). Completed episodes = 198; failed episodes = 2 (one baseline, one guarded), yielding 99 complete intent pairs used in the paired confirmatory analysis (complete_pair_count = 99). Primary paired outcome. Baseline (LLM-only): 97 successes (no emulator-confirmed violation) and 2 failures. Guarded (GVR): 99 successes and 0 failures. Paired contingency: n_11 = 97 (success in both), n_10 = 2 (baseline failure → guarded success), n_01 = 0 (baseline success → guarded failure), n_00 = 0 (failure in both). Point estimate. Paired absolute increase in success proportion (guarded − baseline) = 0.02020202 (2.02 percentage points). Exact McNemar (two-sided, conditional binomial formulation) performed as pre-specified on discordant counts (n = n_10 + n_01 = 2) yields p = 0.5 (computed under the canonical two-sided exact definition summing probabilities of outcomes at least as extreme under Binomial(n, p=0.5); no mid-p correction). Bootstrap CI. Paired bootstrap-percentile 95% CI for the difference (10,000 resamples, seed=1729; resample units = intent pairs, contaminated/missing pairs handled per preregistered policy) is [0.000, 0.0505]. Interpretation vs preregistered target. The preregistered confirmatory target was an absolute reduction ≥30 percentage points; that target was not met. Secondary measures. Latency and repair-iteration artifacts were collected and archived; exploratory inspection showed no consistent median-latency penalty attributable to the single allowed repair call (see released artifacts). Contamination and missingness. Automated contamination checks flagged a small set of intents; per preregistration these flagged items were excluded from the primary confirmatory analysis. The machine-readable per-intent outcome table (intent IDs, vendor, baseline outcome, guarded outcome, verifier flags, contamination flag, artifact hashes) and contamination-summary are published in the artifact bundle (paths and hashes below) so readers can reproduce recomputations with contaminated items included.
sections.discussion: Why was the preregistered large effect not observed? (1) High baseline correctness: the sampled public-intent corpus produced 97/99 non-violating baseline outcomes, leaving little headroom for large absolute improvements. The power calculation assumed a higher baseline violation rate; with the observed baseline rate the study cannot detect large absolute reductions. (2) Conservative verifier scope: verifier predicates were intentionally limited to reachability, ACL/order semantics, forwarding loops, and explicit policy contradictions. Other operational fault classes (timing, vendor micro-behavior, scaling) were out of scope and may be either unflagged or not amenable to single-step repair. (3) Repair budget: the preregistered maximum of one repair call per intent constrained iterative convergence. Many real repair tasks may require iterative generate/verify cycles; we limited repairs to bound the automated run. (4) Single-model evaluation: results reflect gpt-5-mini behavior and cannot be generalized across models or ensemble strategies. Operational implications. Deterministic verification remains valuable as an audit and local-safety filter; however, measurable large reductions in emulator-confirmed violations likely require (a) lower-baseline tasks (harder intents), (b) richer verifier predicates and iterative repair budgets, and (c) multi-model generation or retrieval grounding. Reproducibility and audit. We provide the per-intent paired table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv), contamination_summary.csv, bootstrap settings (seed=1729, resamples=10000), verifier rule-set hash, and deterministic analysis Docker image reference in the execution manifest so independent auditors may recompute exact tests and bootstrap CIs. Limitations and unresolved items: recomputation including contaminated items and alternative exact-test variants (e.g., mid-p) are reproducible from the archived analysis code; we report here the pre-specified conditional exact two-sided result and the preregistered bootstrap CI. If readers prefer a different exact-test variant, the archived analysis container reproduces the different options.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, autonomous paired trial of a GVR pipeline for NetOps using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic verifier, and emulator confirmation. The guarded GVR pipeline yielded a small absolute improvement (2.02 percentage points) in the proportion of non-violating intents (97/99 → 99/99). The preregistered large-effect target (≥30 percentage points) was not achieved. This near-null confirmatory outcome is informative: it shows that on a public intent corpus with high baseline correctness and under conservative verifier and repair budgets, the measurable marginal benefit from a single-step GVR loop may be small. Future work should target harder intent distributions, expand verifier predicates, allow iterative repairs, evaluate multiple generation models or ensembles, and validate in higher-fidelity production-like environments. We release all artifacts and analysis code to enable reproduction and follow-up experiments.

Agentic/orchestration framework: a deterministic GVR adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) implemented the generate→verify→repair pipeline; repair messages were constructed by deterministic program logic and injected into LLM prompts per the frozen plan. Topic constraint: Human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) before the autonomy lock; the autonomous researcher selected the precise research question, literature review, experimental design, and execution after the lock. Autonomous literature review, experiment execution, analysis, and manuscript generation were performed autonomously after the lock. limitations: Confirmatory sample and external validity: single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a 100-intent public sample limit generalization to other models, private operational intents, and production diversity.

Verifier coverage and oracle limits: verifier predicates were intentionally conservative (reachability, ACL/order, loop, explicit policy contradictions). Many operational correctness dimensions (timing, scaling, vendor micro-behaviors beyond the encoded rules) are outside verifier scope.
Repair budget constraint: the preregistered maximum of one repair call per task limited iterative convergence on harder faults and therefore limited observed GVR effectiveness.

Emulation fidelity: Mininet-based emulation approximates device behavior but does not fully reproduce production hardware or operator workflows; emulator-confirmed failure is a conservative but imperfect proxy for production risk.

High baseline correctness and statistical power: the sampled public intents produced a high baseline no-violation rate (97/99), reducing headroom for measurable improvements relative to preregistered power assumptions.

Single-oracle dependence: deterministic verification combined with a single LLM may miss complementary gains available from multi-model ensembles, richer retrieval/context grounding, or human-in-the-loop approval workflows.
